questions.stem:
A small ball is thrown vertically upwards with speed $14.7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from a point that is $19.6\,\mathrm{m}$ above horizontal ground. The ball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity.

Find

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) the total time from when the ball is thrown to when it first hits the ground,
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Complete method to find the total time, e.g. $-19.6 = 14.7t+\frac{1}{2}(-9.8)t^2$ using one equation, OR: $0 = 14.7-9.8t_1 \Rightarrow t_1=1.5$, $s_1 = 14.7\times1.5-\frac{1}{2}\times9.8\times1.5^2 = 11.025$, $30.625 = \frac{1}{2}\times9.8\times t_2^2 \Rightarrow t_2 = 2.5$, $t=t_1+t_2=4$ (s), and many other methods.
A1: There are two A marks for all the equations they use, −1 each error.
M(A)1: There are two A marks for the equation(s) that they use, −1 for each error.
A1: $t=4$ (s) only. N.B. If using a quadratic, ignore the other solution, even if it's incorrect. If they combine the 2 solutions in some way, A0

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) the speed of the ball immediately before it first hits the ground,
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Complete method to find the speed. A1: Correct equation(s), e.g. $v^2=14.7^2+2(-9.8)(-19.6)$ OR $v=14.7+(-9.8)\times4$. A1: Speed $=24.5$ or $25$ ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), must be positive.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) the total distance travelled by the ball from when it is thrown to when it first hits the ground.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Method to find a relevant distance, e.g. $0^2=14.7^2+2(-9.8)s$ or $24.5^2=2\times9.8s$. A1: A correct relevant distance, $s=11.025$ (11 or better) or $s=30.625$. M1: Method to find the total distance. A1: Total distance $=2\times11.025+19.6$ or $=2\times30.625-19.6 = 41.7$ (3 sf) or $42$ (2 sf) (m).

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Sketch a velocity-time graph for the motion of the ball from when it is thrown to when it first hits the ground.

State the coordinates of the start point and the coordinates of the end point of your graph.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: Straight line starting on the $v$-axis and crossing the $t$-axis (line may be reflected in the $t$-axis) (B0 if solid vertical line at $t=4$). B1: Correct appropriate coordinates (start point) $(0,14.7)$, allow these to be marked on the axes. B1ft: Correct appropriate coordinates (end point) $(4,-24.5)$, ft on their answers to (a) and (b), allow these to be marked on the axes.

questions.stem:
Figure 1

A particle of mass $10\,\mathrm{kg}$ is placed on a fixed rough inclined plane. The plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$. The particle is held in equilibrium by a force of magnitude $P$ newtons, which acts up the plane, as shown in Figure 1. The line of action of the force lies in a vertical plane that contains a line of greatest slope of the plane. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is $\frac{1}{2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the normal reaction between the particle and the plane.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: $R=10g\cos\alpha$, allow sin/cos confusion. A1: Correct answer $=78.4$ or $78$ (N). Allow $8g$.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the greatest possible value of $P$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: $F=0.5R$ seen anywhere. M1: Correct number of terms, with $10g$ resolved: $P=10g\sin\alpha+F$. A1: Correct equation or inequality. A1: $=98$. Allow $10g$. For any inequality which never becomes an equation, usual rules: Max M1A1A0 for $P\leqslant 10g\sin\alpha+F$.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the least possible value of $P$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Correct number of terms, with $10g$ resolved: $P=10g\sin\alpha-F$. A1: $=19.6$ or $20$. Allow $2g$. For any inequality which never becomes an equation, usual rules: Max M1A0.

questions.stem:
Figure 2

A non-uniform beam $AB$ has length $8\,\mathrm{m}$ and mass $M\,\mathrm{kg}$.

The centre of mass of the beam is $d$ metres from $A$.

The beam is supported in equilibrium in a horizontal position by two vertical light ropes. One rope is attached to the beam at $C$, where $AC=2.5\,\mathrm{m}$ and the other rope is attached to the beam at $D$, where $DB=2\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in Figure 2.

A gymnast, of mass $64\,\mathrm{kg}$, stands on the beam at the point $X$, where $AX=1.875\,\mathrm{m}$, and the beam remains in equilibrium in a horizontal position but is now on the point of tilting about $C$.

The gymnast then dismounts from the beam.

A second gymnast, of mass $48\,\mathrm{kg}$, now stands on the beam at the point $Y$, where $YB=0.5\,\mathrm{m}$, and the beam remains in equilibrium in a horizontal position but is now on the point of tilting about $D$.

The beam is modelled as a non-uniform rod and the gymnasts are modelled as particles.

Find the value of $M$.
(8)

parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Use of $T_2=0$ seen or implied. M1: Correct number of terms, dimensionally correct equation in $M$ and one unknown length (allow without $g$'s, omission of a length is an M error): $M(C), 64g\times0.625=Mg(d-2.5)$ OR e.g. $M(C), 64g\times0.625=Mgx$. A1: Correct equation in $M$ and $d$ only or another unknown length. M1: $S_1=0$ seen or implied. M1: Correct number of terms, dimensionally correct equation in $M$ and same unknown length (allow without $g$'s, omission of a length is an M error): $M(D), 48g\times1.5=Mg(6-d)$ OR e.g. $M(D), 48g\times1.5=Mg(3.5-x)$. A1: Correct equation in $M$ and $d$ only or same unknown length. DM1: Solving for $M$, dependent on all previous M marks. A1: Correct exact answer $M=32$ exact answer.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Other equations: ($T_1$ would then have to be eliminated to give an equation in $M$ and $d$ only, to earn the M mark) $T_1 = Mg + 64g$; $M(A), 64g\times1.875 + Mgd = 2.5T_1$; $M(G), 64g\times(d-1.875) = T_1\times(d-2.5)$; $M(D), 64g\times4.125 + Mg(6-d) = 3.5T_1$; $M(B), 64g\times6.125 + Mg(8-d) = 5.5T_1$; $M(X), Mg(d-1.875) = 0.625T_1$
- Other equations: ($S_2$ would then have to be eliminated to give an equation in $M$ and $d$ only, to earn the M mark) $S_2 = Mg + 48g$; $M(A), 48g\times7.5 + Mgd = 6S_2$; $M(C), 48g\times5 + Mg(d-2.5) = 3.5S_2$; $M(G), 48g\times(7.5-d) = S_2\times(6-d)$; $M(B), 48g\times0.5 + Mg(8-d) = 2S_2$; $M(Y), Mg(7.5-d) = 1.5S_2$

questions.stem:
A particle $P$ is moving in a plane with constant acceleration.
The velocity, $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, of $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$\mathbf{v} = (7-5t)\mathbf{i} + (12t-20)\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Put $t=2$ to give $-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}$. Allow column vectors. M1: Finding the magnitude of their $\mathbf{v}$: $\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}$, the − sign is not required. A1: $5$ ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find, to the nearest degree, the size of the angle between the direction of motion of $P$ and the vector $\mathbf{j}$, when $t=2$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: For a relevant trig equation, e.g. $\tan\theta=\frac{3}{4}$. A1ft: A correct equation follow through on their $\mathbf{v}$. A1: Correct answer (must be in degrees to nearest degree) $37^\circ$ or $323^\circ$.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The constant acceleration of $P$ is $\mathbf{a}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

(c) Find $\mathbf{a}$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Collecting terms in $t$ and constant terms (may be implied): $\mathbf{v}=(7-5t)\mathbf{i}+(12t-20)\mathbf{j}=(7\mathbf{i}-20\mathbf{j})+t(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})$. M1: Rearranging to required form: $\frac{\mathbf{v}-(7\mathbf{i}-20\mathbf{j})}{t}=(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})$. A1: Correct answer (isw if they find the magnitude). OR: M1: Finding the initial velocity or some other specific velocity: $t=0, \mathbf{v}=7\mathbf{i}-20\mathbf{j}$. M1: Use of $\mathbf{a}=\frac{\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}}{t}$ with $t=2$ (or possibly another appropriate value): $\frac{(-3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})-(7\mathbf{i}-20\mathbf{j})}{2}=(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})$. A1: Correct answer (isw if they find the magnitude). OR: M2: Differentiate wrt $t$. A1: $\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}=\mathbf{a}=(-5\mathbf{i}+12\mathbf{j})$.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find the value of $t$ when $P$ is moving in the direction of the vector $(-5\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j})$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Attempt at equation in $t$ only, using ratio of components, allow reciprocal and a sign error: $\frac{(7-5t)}{(12t-20)}=\frac{-5}{8}$. A1: Correct equation. M1: Solve for $t$ (equation must have come from considering ratios). A1: $t=2.2$.

questions.stem:
Figure 3

A railway engine of mass $1500\,\mathrm{kg}$ is attached to a railway truck of mass $500\,\mathrm{kg}$ by a straight rigid coupling. The engine pushes the truck up a straight track, which is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\sin\alpha=\frac{7}{25}$. The coupling is parallel to the track and parallel to the direction of motion, as shown in Figure 3.

The engine produces a constant driving force of magnitude $D$ newtons. The engine and the truck experience constant resistances to motion, from non-gravitational forces, of magnitude $1200\,\mathrm{N}$ and $500\,\mathrm{N}$ respectively.

The thrust in the coupling is $2000\,\mathrm{N}$.

The coupling is modelled as a light rod.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the acceleration of the engine and the truck.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme: M1 A2: Using equation(s) of motion to give an equation in $a$ only, with correct number of terms and $500g$ resolved, condone sign errors: $2000-500-500g\sin\alpha=500a$ (truck). (A1: Equation with at most one error; A1: Correct equation.) A1: $a=0.256$ or $0.26$ ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$) ($32/125$ is A0).

parts.label: b
parts.mark_scheme: M1 A2: Using an equation of motion to give an equation in $D$ and $a$ only, with correct number of terms and $500g$ (or $1500g$) resolved, condone sign errors: $D-1200-500-1500g\sin\alpha-500g\sin\alpha=2000a$ (system) OR: $D-1200-1500g\sin\alpha-2000=1500a$ (engine). (A1: Equation with at most one error, $a$ does not need to be substituted, treat omission of $g$ as one error; A1: Correct equation.) A1: $D=7700$. N.B. They may write down the system and engine equations and then: (a) solve them for $a$ (b) solve them for $D$.

questions.stem:
Figure 4

One end of a light inextensible string is attached to a particle $A$ of mass $5m$. The other end of the string is attached to a particle $B$ of mass $3m$. The string passes over a small, smooth, light fixed pulley. Particle $A$ is held at rest with the string taut and the hanging parts of the string vertical, as shown in Figure 4.

Particle $A$ is released.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find, in terms of $m$ and $g$, the magnitude of the force exerted on the pulley by the string while $A$ is falling and before $B$ hits the pulley.
(8)
parts.mark_scheme: M1 A1: $5mg-T=5ma$ OR $5mg-T=-5ma$. M1 A1: $T-3mg=3ma$ OR $T-3mg=-3ma$. DM1: Solve for $T$, dependent on previous two M marks, and must be in terms of $m$. A1: $T=\frac{15mg}{4}$ oe (allow unsimplified and not in terms of $mg$ at this stage). M1: Force on pulley $=2T$ (correct method). A1: $\frac{15mg}{2}$ oe (must be a single positive term).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) State how, in your solution to part (a), you have used the fact that the pulley is smooth.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: The tension is the same on both sides of the pulley. Any equivalent statement. B0 if any incorrect extras. B0 if pulley not mentioned.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Tension is same across the pulley

Figure 5

The acceleration-time graph shown in Figure 5 represents part of a journey made by a car along a straight horizontal road. The car accelerated from rest at time $t=0$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the distance travelled by the car during the first $4\,\mathrm{s}$ of its journey.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme: M1: Complete method to find distance travelled in first 4 s. Must be area of a triangle from a $v$-$t$ graph: $s=\frac{1}{2}\times3\times4^2$ OR $s=\frac{1}{2}\times4\times12$. A1: $=24$ (m).

M1 A1ft: Complete method to find total distance travelled in next 20 s. Must be area of a trapezium from a $v$-$t$ graph (they may use a rectangle + triangle): $12\times20+\frac{1}{2}\times1.5\times20^2\ (=540)$ OR $\left(\frac{12+42}{2}\right)\times20$. Correct unsimplified distance, ft on their 12. M1 A1ft: Complete method to find total distance travelled in next 2 s. Must be area of a trapezium from a $v$-$t$ graph (they may use a rectangle + triangle): $42\times2+\frac{1}{2}\times(-4)\times2^2\ (=76)$ OR $\left(\frac{42+34}{2}\right)\times2$. Correct unsimplified distance, ft on their 42. A1 cao: Total $=640$ (m).
